text:
The Trap-Barrier System (ប្រព័ន្ធអន្ទាក់គ្រប់គ្រងសត្វកណ្តុរនៅស្រែ, commonly abbreviated TBS or ធី-ប៊ី-អេស) is a physical rat-management method recommended for lowland rice, especially irrigated and rainfed lowland areas, which together make up roughly 85-86% of Cambodia's rice-growing area according to this source. Rats are described as a major recurring threat to rice in Southeast Asia and Cambodia specifically; this source cites research estimating that in a bad outbreak year, rat damage can destroy enough rice to have fed roughly 50,000 people for a year.

How TBS works: a small plot of an early-maturing rice variety (the 'trap crop', ដំណាំអន្ទាក់) is planted roughly 2-3 weeks earlier than the surrounding fields, inside a plot of about 25m x 25m. Because it heads and ripens before neighboring fields, it lures in rats from the surrounding area. A plastic sheet barrier (របាំងផ្លាស្ទិច), roughly 0.7-0.8m tall, surrounds this trap-crop plot, and several multi-entry, live-catch cage traps (typically 5-8 per TBS unit, called អងគប់) are set at intervals along the barrier, so rats trying to reach the attractive early rice are funneled into the traps instead of climbing over.

Site selection: for best results, a TBS unit should be placed where there is a documented history of heavy rat damage (ideally over 10% crop loss in the area), surrounded by roughly 10 hectares of rice fields with the TBS positioned near the center of that catchment area, in a spot where water can be controlled/drained, and pre-flooded and drained about 2-3 weeks ahead of the barrier crop's planting so the site is ready in time.

Cost and impact (illustrative figures from this source, not exact guarantees): each TBS unit costs roughly $35-50 (USD) to build, not counting labor or materials a farmer can source locally themselves, and the cage/barrier materials can typically be reused across 2-4 rice-growing seasons. Field research cited in this source associated a single well-placed TBS with protecting yield across roughly 10 hectares and increasing yield by around 0.3-1 ton per hectare in irrigated lowland conditions, though results vary with local rat pressure and how well the system is maintained. The method is recommended for areas where rat damage regularly exceeds about 10%, and works best when organized and shared as a community effort rather than attempted by a single farmer alone, both for cost-sharing and to sustain the practice over time.

Note for KB maintenance: this is a detailed, dedicated CARDI/MAFF technical standard on rat trap-barrier systems, more thorough than a general pest summary. It should be treated as the primary source for TBS content going forward, and used to resolve the previously flagged overlap between pest_rats_biology.json and an earlier standalone trap-barrier-system file - those two should be reviewed against this entry and consolidated or cross-referenced rather than left as separate near-duplicates.
